frameworks.name: ICE Prioritization Framework
frameworks.definition: A three-variable scoring model (Impact, Confidence, Ease) used to rank business initiatives by expected return per resource allocated; maps to Hormozi's four-element value equation (dream outcome, perceived likelihood, time to achieve, effort required).

frameworks.name: BAMFAM (Book A Meeting From A Meeting)
frameworks.definition: A scheduling method where a rebooking appointment is made at the moment the customer completes their current appointment, rather than relying on the customer to self-schedule later.

frameworks.name: Shotgun Offer Partnership Exit
frameworks.definition: A buy-sell mechanism where one partner proposes a price at which they will either buy the other out or be bought out themselves, creating a fair market-clearing price without negotiation asymmetry.

frameworks.name: Six-Title Career Ladder for Technicians
frameworks.definition: A compensation and titling progression (Junior Technician -> Technician -> Senior Technician -> Junior Artist -> Artist -> Senior Artist) with pay bumps every three months and skill unlocks at each level, designed to retain service staff for two-plus years.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for service businesses where customers return on a predictable cycle (e.g., eyelash fills every two to four weeks), booking the next appointment before or during the current appointment, rather than relying on the customer to self-schedule, is an under-exploited lever that can double annual visit frequency if average return interval shortens from five weeks to three weeks.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service business with recurring appointments
Customer needs to return within predictable interval
claims.mechanism: Rebooking while the customer is present eliminates the administrative friction and memory decay that cause delayed or missed returns; the customer has no competing priority in the moment.

numbers.axis: annual visit frequency by rebooking method

bounded_by: Does not eliminate need for sales training to handle objections like 'I'll book later'

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when a service business has clear temporal supply constraints (specific high-demand days or times), raising prices on those peak windows by 10-20% and framing off-peak rates as a discount smooths the demand curve, improves staff utilization on slow days, and increases overall revenue without acquiring new customers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Brick-and-mortar service business
Demonstrable demand concentration on specific days or times
Staff capacity is fixed short-term
claims.mechanism: Higher peak prices create an incentive for price-sensitive customers to shift to off-peak slots; the resulting demand smoothing increases utilization during slow periods while peak revenue per appointment rises.

numbers.axis: revenue impact of 10% weekend price increase at 50% weekend appointment share

bounded_by: Requires customer-facing framing as off-peak discount, not peak surcharge, to avoid backlash
Does not apply to businesses with flat demand distribution across the week

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for beauty and personal care services, the promotional front-end offer (e.g., $99 intro set) functions as a lead magnet and should be designed to break even or lose money; the economic engine is the upsell to a better service tier or membership, so tracking upsell close rate is more important than tracking front-end close rate.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service business with multi-tier service options
Front-end offer priced for volume, not margin
claims.mechanism: Customers who book the promotional offer have already demonstrated intent and committed payment; they are assumed-closed on the front end. All margin sits in the upsell step, so close rate on the upsell is the true business metric.
bounded_by: Does not apply to single-service businesses with no upsell path

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that structuring a membership upsell as a default opt-out rather than an opt-in (framing it as 'you've already been paying for these benefits and just haven't formalized it') can move upsell close rates from a typical 20-40% to 80-90%, because the psychological default is acceptance rather than decision.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Customer has existing repeat purchase history with the business
Membership benefits are real and observable (not just a discount)
claims.mechanism: Framing leverages the opt-out default effect: people accept defaults at much higher rates than they actively opt into identical choices. Citing the customer's actual visit history as evidence they have 'already opted in behaviorally' removes the perceived risk of the new commitment.

numbers.axis: membership upsell close rate by framing method

bounded_by: Requires genuine prior purchase history to use the behavioral-default framing credibly
Does not apply to first-time customers

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that customers who prepay for multi-month or annual service memberships churn at a significantly lower rate than month-to-month members, accelerate business cash flow, and are effectively locked out of competitive alternatives for the prepaid period, making prepayment upsell the highest-value transaction in a recurring-service business.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Recurring service business with monthly or per-visit billing
Customer has already agreed to membership
claims.mechanism: Prepayment creates a sunk-cost commitment that reduces the psychological ease of canceling; cash collected upfront can be deployed immediately for growth investment rather than waiting for monthly installments.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that business owners who scale to multiple locations by bringing in equity partners before building documented systems and financial capacity to hire managers will produce lower-quality fulfillment, weaker brand consistency, and partnership conflicts that consume more management bandwidth than the additional revenue justifies.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service business expanding to multiple physical locations
Expansion financed by partner equity rather than owner capital or debt
claims.mechanism: Partners taken on for manpower rather than capital or capability are not incentivized to uphold standards they did not build; inconsistent fulfillment depresses word-of-mouth and repeat rates at new locations, making each new location harder to make profitable than the last.
bounded_by: Does not apply when partners bring documented skills or capital that meaningfully accelerate the model

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the fastest path to the first two or three locations is not the fastest path to fifty locations; deliberately slower early expansion with full founder control and documented systems enables more aggressive later scaling because the infrastructure compound.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Multi-location service business
Founder contemplating expansion before systems are documented
claims.mechanism: Early locations built under direct founder control produce a replicable template; locations opened before the template exists require founder firefighting at each site, making the marginal location additive in effort rather than multiplicative in output.
bounded_by: Does not apply to businesses where speed of market capture is the primary moat

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when a working partner is not compensated at market rate for their operating role (e.g., a de facto general manager receiving only an equity profit share), the business's reported profit margins are artificially inflated, and the true unit economics of opening additional locations cannot be accurately calculated.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Multi-partner service business
One partner performing managerial work without salary separate from profit share
claims.mechanism: The cost of that management labor is missing from the income statement; when the business eventually replaces the working partner with a paid hire, margin drops and return on capital per new location shrinks. Decisions made on the inflated margin are therefore systematically over-optimistic.

numbers.axis: location profitability before and after imputing manager cost

anchors.region: apparent profit (founder doing manager role unpaid)

bounded_by: Does not affect businesses where the founder's role has already been backfilled by a paid hire

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends an equity-swap exit mechanism for multi-location partnerships where both partners jointly own multiple locations: each partner takes full ownership of separate locations rather than buying the other out with cash, resulting in a clean break with no ongoing payments, no tax event on an in-kind transaction, and preservation of the personal relationship.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Two or more partners jointly own stakes in multiple discrete business locations
Both partners are willing to separate
Location margins are approximately equal so the swap is roughly at-value
claims.mechanism: An in-kind equity swap for equity creates no cash obligation, no monthly reminder of the split, and preserves the ability to remain friends and share operational knowledge informally. Cash buyouts strain relationships monthly; equity swaps end the entanglement cleanly.
bounded_by: Does not work when locations have materially different valuations and neither party wants to accept the worse unit
Requires both parties to have separate legal entities for each location

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that giving service employees profit-share bonuses (not equity) for locations they manage, structured as 10% of location profit in year one rising to 20% in year two contingent on reaching a two-year tenure milestone, retains top performers and motivates operator-level accountability without surrendering cap-table equity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service business with multiple locations
Target employee is a high-performing technician with manager potential
Business has additional locations planned that the employee can be placed into
claims.mechanism: Profit share creates financial alignment without triggering the four components of equity (risk, control, profit, exit participation) that most employees neither want nor understand; the two-year vesting cliff filters for commitment and allows performance evaluation before the reward is paid.

numbers.axis: manager profit share by tenure year

bounded_by: Does not work if the business has no additional locations to offer, since part of the incentive is the career path to running a new location

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a six-stage technician title progression with a pay raise every three months (e.g., from 40% to 50% of service revenue over approximately two years) retains service staff longer and produces a natural training pipeline, because frequent visible progress checkpoints prevent the six-to-twelve month resignation window when career stagnation feels most acute.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service business paying technicians on commission percentage
Technician workforce that can exit to self-employment
claims.mechanism: Frequent small promotions (every three months) keep the next milestone visible and close in time; six-month or annual intervals create periods of perceived stagnation that coincide with resignation decisions. Additional skill unlocks at each level increase earning power beyond the percentage bump, compounding the retention value.

numbers.axis: technician commission rate by career stage

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that hiring a dedicated lead-response caller whose single task is to phone inbound web leads within approximately one minute (rather than relying on the booking flow alone) is a two-to-three times revenue multiplier for local service businesses, because most inbound leads that do not immediately confirm an appointment are lost to slow follow-up.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: call the leads within one minute
conditions: Local brick-and-mortar service business
Inbound lead volume sufficient to justify a part-time or full-time caller
Business has an online booking or inquiry flow
claims.mechanism: Leads who fail to complete online booking are the highest-intent pool that can be recovered; immediate phone contact catches them while intent is highest. Delayed contact allows competing alternatives and cold-footing to erode conversion.

numbers.axis: estimated revenue multiplier from adding lead-response caller

bounded_by: Requires sufficient inbound lead volume for the role to be cost-effective

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that daily role-play practice (30 minutes before shift, pairs of staff taking turns as technician and client) is the correct training format for service-staff sales scripts, because passive instruction fails and only high-repetition live simulation builds automatic behavior under actual customer conditions.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service business training staff on upsell or rebooking scripts
Staff interact with customers face-to-face
claims.mechanism: Behavioral automaticity requires repetition under lifelike conditions; reading a script or a one-time demonstration does not build the motor-level habit needed to execute the script when attention is divided during live service delivery. Immediate error-correction ('say it like this, try again') during role-play compresses the feedback loop.
bounded_by: Does not apply to complex consultative sales where scripting reduces conversion

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that collecting customer attribution data (where they heard about the business) at the point of check-in via a standardized intake form is a prerequisite for scaling ad spend, because without channel-level attribution it is impossible to identify which paid or organic sources are generating customers and which are wasting budget.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Multi-channel acquisition (Google ads, organic SEO, referral, social)
Service business considering increasing ad spend
claims.mechanism: Ad spend allocation without attribution data is equivalent to betting on unknown odds; large irreversible bets on channel expansion require measured evidence of what is already working.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi observes that a service business spending 0.5% of revenue on marketing (well below the rough 1% baseline) should suspect either that the current channel is drastically under-funded relative to its demonstrated effectiveness, or that the channel is not producing results at all — in either case, the answer is to measure attribution first before increasing spend.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service business with a measurable inbound channel (e.g. Google)
Marketing spend is below 1% of revenue

numbers.axis: marketing spend as percentage of revenue

anchors.region: rough minimum baseline for local service business

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that offering a membership-level benefit (locked-in non-surge pricing) while simultaneously introducing weekend surge pricing for non-members creates a powerful pull-through mechanism: the price increase manufactures a problem, and the membership solves it, making the membership offer feel compelling rather than optional.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: create a problem then solve it
conditions: Service business introducing dynamic pricing for the first time
Membership product already in design or launched
claims.mechanism: Customers motivated by avoiding the new surge price convert to membership at higher rates than customers pitched on membership benefits alone, because loss aversion (avoiding a price increase) is a stronger motivator than gain framing (getting extra benefits).
bounded_by: Requires that the surge pricing policy be credibly enforced, not softened upon customer pushback

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that rebooking the next appointment and upselling to membership must be treated as distinct sales conversations requiring explicit training and scripts, not administrative tasks, because the revenue impact of achieving 80-90% rebook rates from a baseline of 50-70% is large enough to be a core business initiative.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Recurring-visit service business
Staff trained primarily on service delivery, not sales
claims.mechanism: Service staff who mentally categorize rebooking as administration underinvest in overcoming customer hesitation; reframing it as a sales conversation assigns appropriate training resources and incentive attention to the outcome.

numbers.axis: rebook close rate by staff treatment of the conversation

anchors.value: some clients but not all; roughly 50-70% anecdotal

anchors.region: treated as sales with training and overcoming objections

examples.text: Ani (Amy Lash & Beauty, 7 locations, $2.3M/year, 28% net margin) was spending $1,000/month total on Google Ads split across six locations — approximately $167/location/month, or 0.5% of revenue. She reported that 50% of her clients cited Google as how they found her, suggesting the channel was working but massively under-funded. Hormozi observed this as a likely goldmine: her cost to acquire a customer through Google was probably very low, and she could capture substantially more volume by increasing spend, but first needed attribution tracking to confirm the channel's actual economics before scaling budget.

Hormozi recounted his own experience with six gym locations and multiple partners, mirroring Ani's situation. He stated that if he had continued to cash-flow the first location rather than rapidly expanding into partner-backed new locations, he would have had a stronger brand and better infrastructure before entering new markets. He gave up his best location to a partner in order to cleanly exit a partnership, choosing the short-term asset loss over the ongoing management drag of a misaligned partnership.

Hormozi cited a study from what he recalled as '50 Scientific Ways to Get to Yes' in which one country achieved 80% organ donor opt-in rates versus 10% in comparable countries purely by changing the enrollment form: the high-opt-in country used an opt-out default rather than an opt-in default. He applied this directly to Ani's membership upsell, proposing that framing long-term customers as having already behaviorally opted into the membership (because they return repeatedly) and simply needing to 'formalize' it would replicate the default-opt-out dynamic.

Hormozi described Ani's first partnership: she took on a partner who now has a full-time career elsewhere and a new baby, and who no longer manages lash artists or trains staff. The resulting customer-service and fulfillment gaps at that partner's location correlate with lower customer volume, suggesting word-of-mouth referrals suffer when partner-managed locations deliver inconsistent service. The situation illustrates how misaligned partners, taken on for operational manpower before systems existed, produce outcomes that damage the brand rather than extend it.

Ani reported that she could upsell 90% of clients from a $99 intro set to a $170 set when she personally handled the conversation, but that her team upsold at under 50% and some staff did not ask at all. Hormozi identified this gap as the primary missed revenue opportunity: the front-end $99 offer effectively breaks even after labor and materials, so every upsell converted above the 50% staff baseline was incremental margin not being captured. He framed the $99 as a lead magnet and the upsell as the real business.

practices.text: When a customer hesitates to rebook before or during their appointment, staff should say: 'We have 60 minutes right now, let's just get one thing sorted — when do you want to come back?' and offer two specific dates to choose from rather than asking an open-ended question.

At check-in, ask every customer for their ID (to confirm the appointment), confirm the card on file, and have them complete a sign-in form with a drop-down for how they heard about the business and a referral code field. Do not rely on end-of-visit surveys; capture attribution data at arrival when attention is highest.

For existing recurring clients, frame the membership pitch as: 'You've been here six times in the last six months and haven't been getting any of the free benefits you should have been getting. All you have to do is sign up as a member — you pay nothing more than you currently pay.' Then offer to run the card on file immediately.

After a customer agrees to a monthly membership, follow up immediately with: 'Would you like to save money by prepaying? Would you prefer six months or twelve?' Frame the twelve-month option as 'today's service is free' based on the annual discount, not as a large upfront payment.

When approaching a partnership exit, present the shotgun offer (a price at which you will buy them out or accept being bought out) first; if declined, offer the equity swap as a second option. Prioritize the cleanest break over the best short-term financial outcome, because the management drag of a dysfunctional partnership costs more than a favorable split.

To retain service technicians who might leave to operate independently, tell them explicitly: 'After two years, the best-performing person among all technicians at that stage will be given the opportunity to manage a new location and earn 10% of its profit in year one and 20% in year two.' Frame it as a competitive selection, not a guarantee.

Run daily 30-minute role-play sessions before opening: pair staff, rotate who plays client and technician, and immediately correct errors with 'say it like this — try again' until correct execution happens five times consecutively. Do not use script-reading alone; behavioral automaticity requires live simulation.

Prioritize business initiatives using ICE scores (Impact x Confidence x Ease). Start with the highest-ICE item first regardless of emotional weight. High-impact but low-ease items (e.g., partnership resolution) are not necessarily done last — resolve them early if they are consuming 80%+ of management bandwidth and blocking execution of all other items.
